project.name: Dun
project.boundarySource: Mapped named-place location with a conservative editorial study buffer
project.researchNotes: Full strict-boundary audit. Dun remains selector-only at 24 because House of Dun is a separately scored destination rather than settlement merit. The attraction supplies the only qualifying cafe, trails, picnic, parking and toilets. All 20 local statutory HES records are now visible and materially dated. The 70 NRHE records remain intact: those that identify a cross-linked structure or defensible designed-landscape phase are dated and visible; period-unassigned survey and natural-feature records remain map-hidden rather than guessed. No exact Dun product was found at Treasure Trails, Curious About, Mystery Guides or GoQuest. Angus-wide full audit completed 2026-09-01: all six visitor categories, the four named commercial trail providers, current official/conventional routes, strict-boundary scoring and local HES/NRHE integrity were checked.

touristAppeal.label: Minor Interest
touristAppeal.summary: Dun itself is a sparse parish locality without an independent visitor centre; House of Dun is a separately scored destination and does not inflate the settlement.
touristAppeal.dogAccessSummary: The estate is dog-welcoming with restrictions around livestock, but this belongs to the separate attraction rather than the locality score.

visitorHighlights.name: House of Dun, Garden & Estate
visitorHighlights.reason: A nationally important, fully managed historic-house experience with guided interiors, formal gardens, museum displays, wildlife-rich estate walks and dependable visitor facilities.
visitorHighlights.openingTimes: Estate daily 08:00–20:00; house, café, museum and formal gardens follow published seasonal hours
visitorHighlights.admission: House adult £18.50; garden and estate free; parking £5 for non-members

editorialReview.scoreRationale: A nationally important, fully managed historic-house experience with guided interiors, formal gardens, museum displays, wildlife-rich estate walks and dependable visitor facilities.

townGuide.characterTag: Sparse parish locality beside a major estate
townGuide.headline: A minor locality with one major separate destination
townGuide.intro: Dun scores 24% as a settlement. House of Dun is shown separately in See, with its café, walks and practical facilities, so the attraction is not misapplied to the locality.
perfectFor: Planning a separate House of Dun visit

suggestedFirstVisit.title: Go directly to House of Dun
suggestedFirstVisit.summary: Follow the brown tourist signs rather than treating Dun as a conventional village centre. The attraction has its own car park and visitor facilities.

townGuide.suggestedTime: Pass-through locality; 3–5 hours for the separate attraction
townGuide.visitorMood: Attraction-led countryside rather than a visitor town.

features.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
features.reviewNotes: Material period verified as Later prehistoric settlement and roundhouse; map name unchanged.
features.fullDescription: The monument comprises the remains of a palisaded enclosed settlement and a ring ditch house of prehistoric date represented by cropmarks visible on oblique aerial photographs. The monument lies on relatively level, well-drained ground at around 50m OD overlooking the Montrose basin to the S. It comprises two elements. A sub-circular palisaded enclosure some 40m in diameter is the southern element. There are no definite traces of internal structures within the enclosure although there are numerous amorphous cropmarks which may relate to contemporary deposits. To the NNE of the enclosure is a ring ditch house some 15-18m in diameter with a ditch some 2m wide, representing the remains of a former timber roundhouse. The surrounding area is rich in the remains of prehistoric settlement and economic activity. The area to be scheduled encompasses the visible features and areas around them in which traces of associated activity may be expected to survive. It is divided into two separate circular areas. The S area has a diameter of 80m while the N area has a diameter of 60m, as marked in red on the accompanying map.

features.reviewNotes: Material period verified as Bronze Age, c. 2500–800 BC; map name unchanged.
features.fullDescription: The monument is a burial cairn dating probably to the Bronze Age (between about 2500 BC and 800 BC). It is visible as a large, grass-covered mound. The cairn is situated on a low rise 25m above sea level, overlooking the Montrose Basin which lies about 800m to the SE. The upstanding burial cairn measures around 26m in diameter. The top of the mound has a level surface measuring some 12m in diameter. The cairn stands about 1.6m high from most viewpoints, but appears higher when seen from the E. Water-worn cobbles are visible in places beneath the turf. The scheduled area is circular on plan, measuring 46m in diameter, to include the remains described above and an area around them within which evidence relating to the monument's construction, use and abandonment is expected to survive, as shown in red on the accompanying map. The above-ground elements of the post-and-wire fence surrounding the cairn are specifically excluded from the scheduling to allow for their maintenance. The monument was first scheduled in 1970, but the present amendment provides documents to modern standards.

features.reviewNotes: Material period verified as Neolithic or Early Bronze Age, c. 2000–1500 BC; map name unchanged.
features.documentedDateText: Neolithic or early Bronze Age, about 2000–1500 BC
features.fullDescription: The monument is the surviving portion of a large burial mound of the Neolithic or early Bronze Age, some 3500 to 4000 years old, situated in mature woodland. About half of the mound was removed during the digging of the adjacent quarry in the 19th century, but the portion that remains measures 2.5m high; the mound must originally have been about 20m in diameter. The remaining part of the mound will cover one or more burials, and further burials may have been dug into its surface. The area to be scheduled measures 30m in diameter, modern field boundaries being specifically excluded from the scheduling, as marked in red on the attached map.
